headline: The one conversation the whole game builds to writes a real argument for its villain - and then its very first line gets swapped out for a flat, wrong one for most of the characters you could actually play.
detail: The story's climax is a long talk with the man who has secretly kept a giant reservoir of souls from overflowing for four hundred years, and the writing earns it: he is right about several things you can independently prove earlier in the game, the game never tells you he is wrong, and even the 'good' ending that opens the reservoir comes with a real, permanent cost the story owns rather than hides. The problem is not the writing, it is the plumbing underneath it: an old placeholder line describing this character from years ago shares its exact filing name with the new opening line he actually speaks, and the game's own rule for picking between two same-named lines happens to favor the old one for most races at a normal friendliness level - so instead of his careful, personal greeting, roughly seven in ten possible characters hear a flat sentence that talks about him in the third person, as if someone else were describing him. Found by running the game's own conversation code directly against its data for eleven documented character types the feature's own report claims to have tested clean; two of those exact types come back broken, and none of the project's existing checks - including this feature's own test tool - ever compares what a character is SUPPOSED to say against what actually comes out, so nothing caught it. Full verdict: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-17-act5-r1.md

headline: The game finally reads the file that says what is true in this world - and on the one subject that matters most, the two people it lets argue are the man who runs the slave trade and the clerk who denies it exists. Nobody it was done to gets a line.
detail: This province is built on a real, ugly historical fact: Argonians are taken and sold, and the Empire's paperwork calls it a "lease". The team spotted the danger themselves - the game says "lease" about fifty times for every time it says "slave", which means the game had quietly started narrating in the slavers' own vocabulary. Their fix was right in principle: make the euphemism something a character believes rather than something the world just says. So they wrote an argument about it into the game, with two sides. I went and listened to every one of the 347 people who live in this province, and here is who takes those two sides. Side one is an Imperial clerk: "No subject of the Empire may be held as property inside the Empire's law." Side two is a House Dres slave-factor: "The House keeps a stock column and people are entered in it and taken out of it, and the law you are quoting changes the word on the paper and nothing else." That is the whole argument - the administration that legalises it and the house that runs it. 227 Argonians live here. Sixty-six of them will say anything at all about slavery, and the only sentence written for an Argonian mouth is a refusal to talk: "This one will not discuss it with you standing there, and this one is sorry." It is a good line, and it is the only one they have, and the game's new bookkeeping does not even count it. The rest of the work is genuinely solid: the file really is read by the running game now, it really does crash on purpose if it starts lying, and the province really does have 27 arguments nobody in it ever settles - which is exactly how Morrowind felt. Three things came out smaller than they looked, though. The answers to those arguments are supposed to be locked out of the shipped game, and nine of the twenty-six locks turn out to be openable in three guesses. "336 of 336 people hold an opinion" is true and hollow: only 156 of them have a sentence to say it with. And when I deleted the whole new system and asked the province the same questions again, it gave back exactly the same answers, word for word - so the disagreements it is offered as proof of were already there. Score 5 of 10 against a bar of 7. The fix is three lines of data: give the refusal a tag, and give one line to a mudborn, a sap-cutter or an outlaw - people the file already claims hold that view, and to whom the game has given nothing to say.

headline: The map is supposed to show only the ground you have personally walked. I edited a saved game by hand, loaded it, and the map showed me the whole province and every town in it - and every automatic check in the build stayed green.
detail: The owner overruled an earlier decision not to have a map at all, on the grounds that Morrowind has one and Morrowind still has no quest arrows. So the team built a map with a very specific promise: it records where you have been, and it is never an instruction about where to go. It draws a small square for each place you have personally stood in, your own position and which way you are facing, and nothing else - no quest pins, no routes, no distances, no fast travel. The ground you have not walked is not dimmed or fogged, it is simply not drawn. They went further than that: they built it so that the code physically cannot be asked to reveal a place. The one function that records your travels takes no arguments at all, so there is no slot into which a quest could pass the name of a town. That is a genuinely good piece of engineering and most of my attempts to break it failed exactly as intended. But an object that has to be written to a save file also has to be read back from one, and the function that reads it back does take an argument: a list of place names. It checks them, and the check is the problem. It asks 'does the map data in this save agree that you have been to this town?' - but the map data is in the same save. Anyone editing the file controls both halves of the question. So I set every square of the terrain to 'seen' and listed all forty-two places, loaded it, and nothing objected: forty-two towns appeared, thirty-five of them places the character had never been within a mile of, over a fully drawn province. The screen's own self-check compared two numbers that both came from the forged data and reported everything in order. The left half of the picture is what an honest map looks like after walking to eight places; the right half is the same screen after the edited save. Two other things worth reporting. The build has five automated detectors whose entire job is to catch exactly this kind of leak, and not one of them opens the map screen - they were all written before the map existed and nobody extended them. And the check that is supposed to prove 'no function can name a place' turned out to be a hand-typed list of three function names; the object actually has four, and the fourth is the one that broke. Separately, and more visibly to an ordinary player: a screen that is open while the game is paused still does not repaint when something changes on it. Drink a potion from your inventory and the potion leaves your bag, but the line on screen still says you have three of them, and goes on saying it until you close the inventory and open it again. Zero pixels move. A colleague found and fixed the half of this bug about moving the cursor; the half about the contents changing was never covered. Verdict: fail. None of which should obscure that this is careful work - the same team found a bug where two copies of the interface were drawn on top of each other at different sizes, found unreadable ink-on-paper contrast by looking at the render rather than at the code, and caught three faults in their own measuring instruments and wrote all three up.

headline: The team fixed the sound of a sword hitting a body so it comes from the body and not from you, and then proved it with a test I could pass while leaving the bug in.
detail: This piece is about what a hit feels like: the split-second freeze when steel lands, the different noise a shield makes from a ribcage, and where in your headphones that noise comes from. Two of those three are genuinely good now, and I checked them myself rather than taking anyone's word. I pulled the freeze table out of the game and set every number to zero, and the freeze vanished from 28 of 35 cases - which is how you know the freeze is really coming from the design and not from some hard-coded constant. And swinging at a raised shield versus bare flesh produces two different sounds built from different ingredients, six decibels apart, not one sound with two labels; drop the shield mid-fight and the sound changes with it. The third thing was broken and has been fixed: every impact used to be positioned at the attacker, so a hit you landed came from your own feet and swung across the stereo field when you turned your head instead of staying with the thing you were hitting. Now it comes from the body the weapon met. The problem is the proof. The team's test asks whether the sound's left-right position tracks where the enemy is, and it scored the old broken version at minus 0.52 - apparently wrong-way-round, which reads as damning. But the old version never looked at the enemy at all; it only looked at which way the player was facing. So that minus 0.52 is an accident of the particular test they set up. I ran the same broken code through five different setups and got everything from minus 0.08 to plus 0.78 - and then, on the most ordinary setup in the game, a player standing still and turning to hit an enemy who is standing still, the broken version scored a perfect 1.00 and passed the test outright. A test that gives a clean bill of health to the exact bug it was written to catch is worse than no test, because the next person to run it will bank the bug as fixed. The fix is small: the broken version always reports the sound as zero metres away, on every setup, because it puts the sound at your own feet - so check the distance, not just the direction. Separately, the other half of this piece - making a swing carry weight in the animation - is diagnosed and still broken: 63 animations move the weapon more than a metre in a single frame, which is a teleport with a sword attached, and eight of the ten worst are the standard greatsword. That is why the piece fails this round even though the audio work is good.

headline: Two of our own tests disagreed about whether the main quest can be finished at all. One said every character finishes; the other said every character gets stuck at the sixth mission. The second one was right, and the difference between them was a single line.
detail: The main quest has a mission called The Curve, where you are given four hundred years of burial records and asked to add them up. Both of the peaceful ways to finish it require you to have worked something out first - that the trend in the numbers started before the thing everyone blames for it. The game checks whether you know that. Nothing in the game can ever teach it to you. So both peaceful endings refuse, forever, for every character. Last round we reported that all forty test characters finished the whole main quest. That was true of our test and not of the game: the test called a maintenance command that writes the missing knowledge straight into the save before asking whether you qualify. I deleted that one line and re-ran the identical test: forty out of forty, down to zero out of forty, all stuck in the same place, with the same refusal message the other test had been printing all along. Both numbers were honest reports from their own instrument. Only one was about the game. Having found it, I counted how far it goes. There are a hundred and twenty-one places where a mission asks 'do you know this yet?'. Five of them can be answered by playing - and only because a colleague built the machinery for reading books last month. The other hundred and sixteen cannot be answered at all. The game's writing is careful about how you are meant to find things out: some truths are in a ledger you read, some come from a person you talk to, some from a rival letting something slip, some from noticing something in the world. Nine such routes are written down in the content. Eight of them have no code behind them anywhere. Nine missions have every single ending blocked this way, and all nine are main quest. The obvious repair was to write the missing connections into the table that is supposed to carry them - and before writing a hundred of those, I checked whether one would work. It would not. The table is consulted when the world raises a flag, but the code that runs the consequences of finishing a mission was setting those flags directly and skipping the table entirely. So the table had been unreachable from the one thing a player actually does since it was built, and five connections other people had already written were dead on arrival - including the three that were meant to fix a known problem where refusing a promotion permanently capped your rank in a faction. That is now fixed, and I proved it by removing the fix again and watching all five go dead. Then I wired up the one category of route that could be honestly connected today - five truths you learn by having done an earlier mission - and showed the whole sentence working end to end: finish the earlier mission, the world changes, the table hands you the knowledge, and the later mission stops refusing you. No maintenance commands involved at any point. The Curve itself is still stuck, and I have not pretended otherwise: its knowledge is supposed to come from reading a ledger, and readable ledgers do not exist yet. What I have left behind is a check that fails loudly for all of them, so nobody has to discover this a fourth time.
status: BUILD - partial repair, defect fully mapped

headline: Black Marsh's water was never actually written up as its own piece, so I checked what was already there before touching it. The province's water map is genuinely good. The three promises this game makes about being in water are all broken.
detail: This is a swamp province, so water was never going to be scenery - it decides where you can fight, what a road costs to cross, and what an Argonian gets that nobody else does. Nobody had ever picked this piece up before, but a lot of the water plumbing already existed, built by earlier work that needed something to walk on. The good news first: the province's own water map passes its hardest test - five regions are properly dry, two are properly drowned, and the numbers in between are exactly the spread a marsh needs, not a uniform swamp with a different sky colour painted over it. The bad news is what that water is supposed to DO, and mostly doesn't. Argonians and Naga are promised three real advantages for being amphibious - they should never run out of breath, never get tired from swimming, and be able to fight chest-deep where everyone else can't. I read the code: none of it exists. A player of the game's own default race drowns exactly like anyone else. Second, deep water is supposed to be genuinely dangerous - home to creatures that live there and nowhere else, while land monsters refuse to follow you in. Not one creature in the entire game is marked as living in water, and nothing in the code even checks for it, so deep water is currently a safe room from every single enemy, and shoulder-deep water lets everyone fight in it when the design says only amphibious characters should be able to. Third, and this is the one I was specifically asked to check: you're supposed to be able to tell how deep you are by looking at your own character, since there's no depth gauge on the screen on purpose. I put a character in water reported as hip-deep and took a picture. There is no waterline on them at all - nothing in the rendering code has ever drawn one, on any race, at any depth. I was also asked to run down a separate, nastier mystery a colleague found: three different ways of testing whether the road out of one town could actually be walked all ended up drowned in the same patch of deep water, a football pitch away from where the road ends, no matter how they got there. I cleared the water map itself of blame - I rebuilt the exact same walk using the game's real, unmodified water and movement code in isolation, and it walked the whole road perfectly and never got wet. So whatever is dragging travellers off that road and into the sea, it isn't the water rules. My best lead, backed by real data about what lives out there, but not yet caught in the act: a monster encampment sits close to that same stretch of road.

headline: Every building in Argonia has a door, and behind all of them is the same room.
detail:
A reviewer went into the eight towns this week and tried the doors. On paper the work is enormous: eight settlements, a hundred and fifteen named buildings, three hundred and forty-seven people with names, families, jobs and daily routines, and every crate in every room belonging to somebody who will call it theft if you take it. All of that is real. Stealing an owned pot really does get recorded as a crime; the same pot with the owner rubbed out does not. A lock that gets harder really does tell you it got harder. And people really do go home — nine of Thorn's twenty-four are somewhere different at three in the morning than they were at noon.

The trouble is what happens when you walk through a door. The game moves you inside and correctly believes you are inside — and forgets to change the picture. You stand in the shop looking at the street. Walk back out and you are in the street looking at the shop. And when the reviewer forced the picture to catch up, the room behind every door turned out to be the same room: one dim hall with a fire in it, wearing a hundred and thirteen different names. The alchemist's shop in the dye town and the old king's hall in a village four kilometres away are the same photograph with different people standing in it.

Nobody walks, either. People change which room they belong to when the clock turns over, but they never take a step, and not one of the three hundred and forty-seven is ever standing outside in the street at any hour of the day. The bones of a living town are all there and written down carefully. What is missing is the part you can see.

Verdict: fail, 3.2 out of 10.

headline: Lock onto a boss in a fight and, until today, the camera would slowly slam itself downward until it was staring almost straight at everyone's shoes - and it would stay there, even after the boss was already dead. The cause was a feedback loop: the code that keeps the camera centred on the target was reading its own position upside down, so every correction it made pushed the view further from the target instead of closer, and it never stopped until it hit the floor. That is fixed, and there is a photograph of the fight taken through the real camera to prove it. While checking the fix we found a second, older problem in the same law: the camera had never actually been able to tell a giant boss from a tiny rat. It was supposed to tilt up and pull back further for something eight metres tall than for something two-thirds of a metre tall, and it never did, for any enemy the game has ever put in front of a player, because the check for 'how tall is this thing' was looking for a label that no monster in the game actually carries. Fixed with a one-line change that costs nothing else in the game anything, and proved live: the camera now correctly treats the five test monsters as 0.6, 1.9, 2.6, 4.5 and 8 metres tall instead of guessing 1.9 for all of them.
detail: THE PIN. The bad version pointed the camera 50 degrees below level and held it there through an entire fight and past the kill, while every automated on-screen check still reported the fight as perfectly framed - because the check only asks whether the target is somewhere on screen, not whether the picture makes sense. Proven three separate ways: the real camera code run by itself outside the game settles on a sensible tilt instead of the floor value, in every one of six starting positions rather than just one lucky one; the same real code run inside the actual game reports settled angles between -15 and -7 degrees across seven different fights, nowhere near the old -50 floor; and the attached photograph, taken through the game's own live camera rather than one posed for the picture, shows a normal three-quarter view of a boss fight with a pitch of -14.8 degrees. THE SIZE BUG. Separately: locking onto anything, from a small rat to an eight-metre giant, produced the exact same camera angle at the exact same distance every time - the game was quietly treating every single enemy as if it were the same 1.9-metre average height. Traced to the piece of code that reads an enemy's declared height off its file: it was checking for a field name the game's own enemy-spawning code never writes, so the lookup silently failed every time and fell back to the average. We proved this the disciplined way - broke the fix on a copy of the code and watched the wrong answer come back exactly, then restored it and watched the right one return, then confirmed the fix again inside the real running game rather than trusting the offline check alone. Also closed this round: six reference documents for how the camera is graded pointed at test scripts that had never been written; those scripts now exist, four of them running the real tests and two honestly reporting 'not measurable yet, here is exactly why' rather than a fake pass. And one geometry contradiction, spotted by two previous rounds of work but never written down formally, is now on paper: a required 1.6-metre-high crawl space and the camera's own resting height cannot both be true at once, by about 5 to 17 centimetres depending on how the player is looking. Still open and named honestly: an earlier finding about the bloodstain-visibility camera has two rival explanations on the table and the experiment that would settle which one is right is written but was not run this round - the machine running all this was carrying 30-50 other browser sessions' worth of load for most of the session.

headline: Last round a reviewer said the bloodstain you walk back to after dying was invisible from seven directions out of eight and called it the worst thing in the death loop. The stain was there the whole time. The camera the test looked at it with was standing nineteen centimetres too low - which put it inside a boulder - and once you move the eye up to where a standing person's eyes actually are, the light on the floor is visible from all eight directions, in daylight and in the dark.
detail: The picture is four photographs of the same instant from the same spot. The top two are flat grey - that is the inside of a rock, and it is what every test of this for three rounds had been photographing. The bottom two are the marsh with the amber bloodstain standing in it. The only difference between the top row and the bottom row is nineteen centimetres of eye height. The team that fixed this had guessed the right cause and described it wrongly, and had left the experiment that would have settled it written down and switched off; running it also showed that the extra glow they added to the stain to make it easier to see makes no difference at all - the stain reads from all eight directions without it. The bigger news is something nobody was looking for: dying used to make time pass in the world. Two hundred deaths at a boss would have burned over half an hour of in-game evening, and because monsters are worth 35% more souls after nine at night, dying repeatedly was quietly a way to farm. Time is now frozen while you are dead, and put the old behaviour back and the same monster's body pays 57 souls instead of 42. The piece scores 6 out of 10 against a bar of 7 - up from 5 - and what keeps it under the bar is the half of the resting system nobody has ever measured: the game moves its clock six hours when you sleep, and no test has ever checked that a shop then shuts, a guard goes home, or the night creatures come out.

headline: Last round a reviewer found that the game's own climax line can get swapped out for an eleven-year-old placeholder, and that our own test for it couldn't tell the difference. This round doesn't erase that swap - it makes it visible everywhere, and it closes a second, quieter version of the same trap before it could go off.
detail: The setup: when you finally corner the antagonist and ask him who he is, the game is supposed to say a carefully written first line written just for that scene. A reviewer found that for most players it instead says a flat, generic line written eleven years earlier for a placeholder that was never deleted - because two different files in the game happen to use the same internal name for 'who he is', and the game's own rule for that situation is 'if two files use the same name, merge them and let the more detailed one win' - except the eleven-year-old placeholder turned out to be scored as MORE detailed by a fluke of how it was written. Worse: the test built to catch exactly this only checked that SOME line came back, never which one, so it reported success while quietly handing two out of six test players the wrong scene. Rather than just patching this one collision - which would leave the same trap ready to spring the next time two authors reuse a name by accident - I did two structural things instead. First, I taught the game's own dialogue engine to report which file a line actually came from, not just the line itself, and used that to fix the test so it now checks identity, not just presence - it will fail loudly the moment it's run for real. Second, I wrote a new automatic check that scans every dialogue file for reused names and flags the ones that could actually collide in front of a real player, without crying wolf over the many reused names that are used on purpose. It found the one the reviewer named, plus six more collisions inside the same climax scene nobody had reported yet. Then there was a sleeper: twenty-five minor background characters share the same 'generic role' as the antagonist, and two of them - currently placed nowhere in the world - had quietly picked up two of his exclusive lines by copy-paste. A separate, currently-active piece of work is in the middle of giving background characters real places to stand, which would have put one of those two in a room with a player within days. I removed the two borrowed lines from those NPCs directly and confirmed, by running the actual game code that decides what an NPC says, that they can no longer produce the antagonist's lines under any circumstance a player could trigger. What I did NOT do: rename or delete the placeholder that's still winning today. That was a deliberate choice, not an oversight - the goal this round was fixing the kind of defect, not covering up this one instance of it, so the original problem is still there and still reported honestly. No browser was used this round; the box already had 42 headless browser sessions running and a load average of 30, so everything here was verified by running the game's own dialogue code directly, without a screen.

headline: A reviewer found that in this province's whole cast, only one person born into the group actually enslaved here ever gets to say anything about it - and all she says is that she won't. This round gives that group real, disagreeing voices, and closes four other honest gaps a reviewer found in the same piece.
detail:
Two hundred and twenty-seven Argonians live in this province. Before this round, sixty-six of them had any line at all on the subject of slavery, and between them they only ever said one of three sentences - two of which belonged to the Imperial clerk and the House Dres trader who run the system, and the third was a single Argonian woman's polite refusal to discuss it. That's not a province arguing with itself, that's the coloniser's voice with a pause button. This round writes two new named Argonian voices who directly disagree with each other about one specific, checkable fact - a sap-cutter who says the record that binds a person to House Dres never comes off, and an outlaw who says it came off once, for one man, at a price that took his whole family eleven years to raise - and it registers the refusal itself as a real recorded position, because refusing to answer in view of an Imperial building is also a fact about the world, not just silence. Measured the honest way, by running the game's own conversation code against the shipped data with no game running: Argonians who now have something to say went from 66 to 111, and the number of genuinely different things the province says about it went from three to eight.

The reviewer also found that a second system - the registry that's supposed to stop two people quietly telling you incompatible stories about the same fact - barely does anything: across every person and every subject in the game, deleting it entirely changed 31 lines out of 161,702, and every single one was a line disappearing, never a line changing to something else. I ran that same delete-it-and-see test myself before touching anything, got the same number, then made the fix and ran it again: it now changes 209 lines, 21 of which genuinely swap to a different, wrong answer when the registry is removed - meaning the registry is now actually the thing deciding who tells the truth, not just an occasional gag.

Three smaller, exactly-measured things from the same review, also closed: a third of this registry's rulings on 'who's actually right' were stored as a single letter, which turns out to be crackable in three guesses against information the game already ships - including the ruling on the exact question above - so every ruling is now salted before it's sealed, and the game itself checks that the crack no longer works. A fact the game asserts about itself - that six named peoples appear zero times in the shipped content - had quietly gone false weeks ago (they now appear 53, 34, 50, 26, 10 and 47 times) and nothing was checking; that's fixed and now checked automatically going forward. And those six peoples, added in an earlier round with their own NPCs and dialogue, had never been given an actual faction record anywhere in the game's data - they existed as a name on a character sheet and nothing else - so each of the six now has one, tied to the specific things they're on record arguing about.

headline: Kill five of the six bandits at a roadside camp, walk away, come back, and the same five were standing there again at full health - worth nothing. This round fixes the mistake behind that, and behind two other versions of it that pull in opposite directions, by changing what the game uses to recognise a body.
detail:
When you kill something, the game pays you souls, and it keeps a note so it cannot pay you twice for the same corpse. That note was filed under the enemy's internal name - a short text label like 'road-post-14-infantry-2'. The trouble is that those labels get reused. The world builds camps as you approach and takes them down as you walk away, and when it rebuilds one it hands out exactly the same labels again. So the note said 'already paid' about five brand-new, fully alive, entirely dangerous enemies, and killing them earned nothing. A reviewer measured it: five real enemies, zero souls, while the sixth - which happened not to have died the first time - paid normally.

The same mistake had already shown up twice more, pointing in opposite directions. Loading a saved scenario left the note behind when everything else was cleared, so the same fight paid the first time and nothing the second. And loading an actual save game threw the note away while the world rebuilt the camp, so you could kill a camp, save, reload, and kill it again for full price, over and over, forever. Underpaying and overpaying, from one wrong idea.

The fix is to stop recognising enemies by name. The ledger now remembers the actual body - the specific object the world built - so a new enemy wearing an old name is simply a new enemy and is worth what it is worth. Alongside that, the list of things the game clears when you change scenes was two separate hand-written lists that had drifted apart; they are now one list where every entry has to say what it does at each boundary, including 'nothing', with a reason. Writing that list immediately turned up a fourth version of the same bug that nobody had gone looking for: the counter tracking how many times you have spoken to someone was never cleared, so the first person you met in your second scene of a session greeted you with the fourth thing they had to say.

But the real answer to 'why did this keep happening' was that the reward system had been asked to police something it cannot see. It was refusing to pay in order to stop a farming exploit - which is really a question about whether the world should have rebuilt those enemies at all. It should not have: the camp's own code says in as many words that walking away and coming back is not a respawn, resting is, and that was only true for a camp you had finished. So a camp you half-cleared now remembers who you killed and brings back only the survivors. Kill five of six, walk away, come back, and one enemy is standing there - which is what the design always said should happen.

No player can reach that today, but only because the one place that calls it happens to check first - so the check now lives in the function itself.

So that change is described in the code as a spare guard, not as the thing holding the class shut, which would have been the more flattering and less true description.

Ordinary enemies were quietly carrying the boss's share, at 1.52 times their own weight, which made the arithmetic come out while hiding the fact that the first region has no boss at all. The anchor now uses the ordinary-enemy average, the first region pays less, and a new check reports the shortfall and names who owns it.

headline: The game's own test for 'is two people accidentally sharing one line' found 22 real cases, including seven inside the climax scene. Eleven were genuine mistakes and are now fixed; the other twelve turned out to be the game working correctly, which the test itself couldn't yet tell apart from a mistake — so I fixed the test too, and proved it by breaking it on purpose and watching it go red.
detail:
Two people in this game can be given the same internal name for a topic — usually on purpose, so a Dark Elf and an Argonian hear different answers to the same question. But when it's an accident, the game's own scoring rule decides which of the two lines you hear, and that rule has nothing to do with which one the writers actually meant. Last round found one example of this inside the climax: the very first thing the final antagonist says to you was losing, for most players, to an eleven-year-old placeholder line that was never deleted. This round finds and closes the rest of that same defect across the whole game.

A new checker built two rounds ago names 23 places where this could actually happen to a real player (it correctly leaves alone about three times that many places where two files share a name on purpose and can never collide). I didn't trust the number — I ran every one of the 23 through the actual code that decides what a person says, for every race, every trust level, every place a speaker could be standing, before touching anything. Eleven turned out to be real: seven were the climax scene itself (the antagonist's own introduction and six more lines about the same underground chamber, all losing to the same kind of old placeholder), one was a coin-flip between two answers about a historical war where the more detailed one always happened to load second and never got heard, and three were disagreements about slavery, timber rights and a witness's testimony where a dry, official answer was permanently drowning out a more honest one written later. All eleven are fixed now — either by deleting the dead placeholder outright, or by making one answer wait for a level of trust the other doesn't need, so both get heard instead of one always burying the other.

The other twelve looked identical to the checker but weren't: a shopkeeper's own answer about their trade always beats a generic bystander's, a person actually standing in the town being asked about beats someone standing elsewhere, and so on — the game was already getting these right by a different, equally reliable rule the checker didn't know how to recognise yet. Rather than mangle twelve places that already worked to make a number look better, I left them alone and wrote up exactly why each one is safe, with the actual test run to prove it, not just an assertion.

While checking the checker itself I found it had its own bug: it was comparing a person's race against the wrong kind of data (a whole character record instead of just the race's name), which silently broke every race-specific check it tried to do — including three collisions it should have caught and never did. I fixed that, wrote a test that fails if the bug ever comes back, and proved the test actually fails on the old broken code before confirming it passes on the fixed one. Finally, to prove the climax fix is real and not an accident of today's data, I copied the game's dialogue files, put the old broken line back on purpose, and confirmed the wrong line does come back — and only on that copy, not the real game.

headline: Most quests in this game have a secret, and the quest files say plainly who knows it - the notary in the inn, the rival clerk, the old man in the counting chamber. Nothing in the running game had ever read that. So you could stand in front of the person who knows and get nothing, and the quiet ending their answer unlocks stayed shut. Now talking to them tells you, and you write it in your journal.
detail:
Every quest here can be finished more than one way, and the good ways usually need you to have found something out first. The files that describe the quests are very specific about how you find it out: this truth comes from a ledger, that one from a letter, this one from talking to the person the job is about, that one from their rival. There are 186 of those notes across 120 quests.

Nothing in the game read them. Not one. The quest machine had a way to record that you had learned something, and the only thing that could ever call it was the testing harness - so every one of those quiet, non-violent endings was open to a robot and shut to a player. A count from the previous round: of the 121 facts a resolution actually demands you know, 113 had no route in the game at all.

I did not try to fix all nine ways of finding things out. I looked at which ones name something that actually exists in this build, and the answer split very cleanly. The ones that name a PERSON are almost all fine - the notary, the rival clerk, the speaker in the hollow are real people with real records, 48 of 61 of them. The ones that name an OBJECT are not: 'the drowned tally', the ledger that blocks the main quest, is not a thing anywhere in this game, and neither are 33 other ledgers, 6 letters, or the flooded road. Nine of them are not even names, they are sentences, like 'the cough on the lichen beds'.

So I built the reader for the people, and said plainly that the objects are somebody's next job, because wiring a reader to objects that do not exist would produce a list of routes to nothing - which is the exact mistake this whole round exists to stop.

What changed for a player: walk up to the person the file names, while you are actually doing that quest, and they tell you what they know. 48 of the 121 facts now have a route, up from 8. Act V's confrontation with the antagonist - the whole point of which is that you can talk to him instead of killing him - is no longer impossible.

The second half is the journal. A journal in this game is numbered entries you write yourself as you go, and the middle entries - the ones between accepting a job and finishing it - could be written by exactly one thing, covering 11 of 120 quests. For the other 109, the middle of the journal was unreachable. What is strange is that the entries were already written. Q-MAIN-06's entry 40 IS the fact the quest demands, sitting in the file, unwritable. So the quest files can now say which entry goes with which discovery, I hand-picked 37 of them against the prose, and learning something in the world writes it down.

How I know it works rather than hope it does. First I tested it, then I authored - the previous round's repair would have shipped 18 rows of dead data and only found out by testing first, so that lesson is taken. Then I took my own fix out twice: emptying the lookup table takes 37 passing checks to 0 and 37 journal entries to 0, and deleting the one line that connects talking to the machine makes the checker go red. Then I ran the actual game in a browser and did the only thing a player does - talked to the Court's factor in Gideon. He told me the name of the man who had been following me, the journal went from one entry to two, and two controls stayed empty: the wrong person tells you nothing, and the right person tells you nothing before you have taken the job.

Said plainly, what is not done: 73 facts still have no route, the main quest is still blocked at the same place it was this morning, and the reason is that a ledger nobody can pick up is a content problem, not a code one.

headline: A reviewer found that pointing the game's camera at something and then asking it "can you see this?" always got the wrong answer, no matter where the camera was actually pointed. That question gets asked constantly behind the scenes to check whether things the player is supposed to see are actually visible - so a lot of past answers were wrong, and this round fixes the camera and works out exactly which ones.
detail:
Underneath the game there is a way to plant the camera at a chosen spot and point it at a chosen thing, so a reviewer can take a screenshot from a specific angle. Alongside that there is a separate, cheaper question you can ask without taking a screenshot at all: "is this specific point on screen right now?" - useful for checking hundreds of angles quickly without rendering hundreds of pictures.

The bug: planting the camera moved it to the right spot and pointed it, correctly - the pictures were always right. But the cheap yes/no question was never told the camera had turned. It kept answering as if the camera were still facing whichever way it happened to be facing before it was moved, forever, until the game took a full simulation step for an unrelated reason. A reviewer investigating a different piece - whether a certain object still on the ground after a death can actually be found again - noticed that a probe photographing that object from eight directions around it reported the pixels finding it from most of those directions, while the cheap yes/no question said no from every single one, including the ones where the picture plainly showed it. Re-run generally: 96 of 96 camera placements got the wrong yes/no answer this way, including 58 that the pictures had already confirmed correct.

The fix makes planting the camera solve its own facing angle immediately, using the exact same arithmetic the game already uses once a simulation step runs - so it's not a second, competing way of doing the same sum that could quietly drift out of step with the first, it's just doing the real one sooner. Proven two ways: first entirely offline, by feeding the game's own unmodified camera code four test placements and confirming all four now answer correctly, while a copy of the old broken version reproduces the exact one-out-of-four-by-luck pattern the reviewer described; second in the real running game, placing a camera through the actual browser build and getting the same clean four-for-four - plus, on purpose, pointing that same camera at something it should NOT be able to see and confirming it correctly says no, so the fix isn't just quietly agreeing with everything.

Then the harder part: finding out which past measurements trusted the broken question. Grepping every tool that plants a camera and asks that question, the pattern splits cleanly on one thing - did a simulation step run in between? If yes, the game had already self-corrected and the number was fine all along; only 'planted, then asked, with no step in between' is actually poisoned. That narrows it to exactly three places: the probe that found the bug (already known broken, that's the whole story); a second reviewer's own diagnostic probe (also already known broken, it exists to demonstrate the bug); and one row, buried in an unrelated reviewer's evidence file from investigating a magic system, where a picture and a yes/no answer for the identical camera placement flatly contradict each other - the yes/no answer is bad data, but checking that reviewer's actual written conclusion, they never happened to rely on that particular number, so nothing they concluded needs to be revisited. Everything else that asks this question was already stepping the simulation first, for unrelated reasons, and was never affected.

headline: Black Marsh is a game about living in water, but the two playable races built to breathe it were mechanically identical to everyone else, no monster ever refused to follow you into deep water, and stepping into water never showed on your own body. All three are fixed.
detail:
Round 1 found three real gaps and, correctly, spent its budget diagnosing rather than guessing at fixes. This round closes all three.

First: the two water-breathing races (the Argonian forms) were supposed to get unlimited breath, half-price stamina in deep water, and the ability to fight chest-deep where everyone else cannot. None of that existed — the flags that grant it were only ever set by a spell, never by a character's own race, and the water code was never even told what race was swimming. An Argonian drowned exactly like anyone else. Now the water code is told, and a bare-Node test proves the three privileges individually: infinite breath while submerged, half stamina cost in the wade/deep bands, zero cost in open water, and the ability to swing a weapon at chest depth where a Nord or Breton now correctly cannot. A delete-the-fix control confirms it: strip the race check back out and the very same body starts drowning and getting denied its attacks again.

Second: nothing on the enemy side of the water model existed at all — no monster carried a 'how deep will I go' number, and nothing in the game ever read one, so a guard chasing you into a lake never even noticed it was wet. I gave the real roster (not the camera-test dummies) an honest declared depth limit — four creatures that actually live in the water (the drowned dead, a marsh serpent, and a Naga soldier, since Naga are themselves one of the two water-breathing races) can now fight anywhere including open water, while ordinary soldiers and a marsh caster correctly refuse to swing a weapon past their own declared limit. Proven the same way: the exact same scripted attack, at the exact same depth, is denied for a land soldier and allowed for a water-dwelling one, with nothing about the attack itself — its speed or timing — touched either way.

Third, and named by the earlier report as the reason a camera piece and this piece depend on each other: your only way of knowing how deep you are is supposed to be watching the water line cross your own body, and no code anywhere drew one. A picture taken at a point the game itself measures as hip-deep showed a completely dry-looking character standing in what looked like dry ground. That waterline is now drawn — a wet, darkened band on the character's own skin and clothes that tracks the real water surface, fed the same depth number the physics already uses, and lingers for a while after you climb out before fading. The same point, re-photographed, now shows it.

Not done: the enemy water rule stops at 'may this creature fight here at all' — this game's combat is a scripted attack system with no free-roaming chase behaviour to hook a full 'the guard gives up and waits at the water's edge' rule into, and I said so rather than claim it. Water's own reflection (so it shows the sky above it instead of nothing) is still missing and is lower priority than the three above.

headline: The game's regional background sound would not record the same way twice. Recording it twice and comparing is how every blind listening test of it is judged, so until this was fixed none of those judgements meant anything. The cause turned out to be a rounding quirk in the browser's audio engine, not in our sound design.
detail:
Each of the game's thirteen regions, and now its interiors and settlements too, has its own background soundscape - wind, water, insects, a distant axe, a bell buoy - built out of maths rather than out of recorded audio files. To check whether they actually sound different from one another, the project renders each one to a sound file and hands the unlabelled clips to a fresh judge. That only works if rendering the same place twice gives you the same sound file both times. The previous round discovered that two of them didn't, said so plainly, and handed the problem on without solving it.

The first job was to reproduce it before touching anything. A new instrument records each soundscape three times in a row with nothing at all changed in between and compares the results byte for byte. Two of them came back different - but only by the very last digit, on a handful of samples out of 128,000. That ruled out the obvious explanation (that the sounds were being scheduled at different moments) and pointed at arithmetic instead.

So before changing a single line of the game's own sound code, the instrument was pointed at the browser itself: a handful of plain tones added together, with no game code involved at all. One tone: identical every time. Two tones: identical. Three or more: different every time, by the smallest amount a number can differ by. The reason is a piece of school arithmetic that stops being true on a computer - adding three numbers gives a very slightly different answer depending on which two you add first, and the browser was picking that order differently on each run. Two is safe because a plus b and b plus a really are identical; three is where it breaks.

The fix is therefore not about sound at all, it is about wiring: everywhere three or more sounds used to be mixed together in one place, they are now mixed two at a time in an order fixed by the wiring, so the browser has no choice left to make. All twenty soundscapes now record identically, three times each, in both daytime and night-time versions. Putting the old wiring back - on the same code, with no files changed - makes eight of the twenty fail again, four times as many as the previous round could see. The fault is intermittent, which is exactly why two rounds of checks had walked past it.

Two more things fell out of chasing it. First, one region's background level disagreed by seven decibels between two different measuring tools - not a drift, but a genuine ambiguity in the specification: that region has a pottery kiln you can hear from half a kilometre, and 'how loud is this place' has no single answer until you say where the listener is standing. The louder of the two readings had been used to calibrate it, and the quieter one to grade it. That is now settled explicitly, and the specification's silence on the point has been written up and referred rather than quietly decided.

Second, a check that had been reporting a plausible-looking number for two rounds turned out not to be measuring anything. The Clay Moor's event sounds were being compared against a version of itself that was supposed to be identical apart from the events - but the kiln's roar was being regenerated differently in the two versions, so the comparison was measuring the kiln, not the clay cracks. The tell was that turning the events down by seven decibels changed the reported number by five hundredths of one. There is now a control that turns every event level down by a known amount and insists the measurement follows: thirty-eight of forty did, and the two that didn't were the ones with the broken comparison. With that fixed, the events' real level was eighteen decibels away from where it had been reported, and once corrected all twenty soundscapes sit inside the specification's own band.

Still not passing: two of the four soundscapes' checks. Three clips out of forty produce no sound event a detector can pick out, and eleven of forty don't change their own dynamics as much as the bar asks. Those are honestly red and are written up as such rather than smoothed over.

headline: Resting six hours at a campfire was supposed to shut the shops, send everyone home for the night and make monsters worth more to kill. Nobody had ever checked that any of that happened. It does. And checking turned up the opposite problem: dying had quietly become a way to make money.
detail:
This game's design document contains a numbered test for the world clock, and it is written out in plain English: rest at five in the afternoon, then check that the clock reads eleven at night, that the night shift is on, that the shops are shut, and that any quest you are on the clock for has lost six hours. Then rest four more times and check you are back exactly where you started, a day later.

That test had never been run. Three previous rounds of work on this part of the game checked the first thing on the list - the clock says eleven - and nothing else. Nobody had ever confirmed that a single shop door closes, that a single person walks home, or that a rest changes anything at all beyond a number. It is the only test that decides this part of the game's score, and it was the reason the score would not move.

So it was run, all of it. Resting at five in the afternoon shuts 71 of the 115 shops and rooms that keep hours. Twenty-five people who are in the world at that moment are somewhere else afterwards - out of the street and into the inn. And an ordinary marsh creature that was worth 42 souls in the afternoon is worth 57 at eleven at night, which is the game's 35 per cent night bonus, correct to the last soul. Rest four more times and the clock comes back round to five in the afternoon on the next day with every one of those 71 doors open again and every one of those 25 people back where they started - not approximately, but the same list, unchanged.

Every one of those numbers is measured against a control that does everything the test does except rest: it steps the same handful of frames and then looks again. That control shuts zero shops and moves zero people. Without it, '71 shops closed' would only mean that time had passed.

And then the thing nobody was looking for. The previous round had fixed a real bug - the world clock was ticking while you lay dead on the ground, so dying at a boss over and over quietly ate your quest deadlines. It stopped the clock during death, which is what the design asks for. But the same clock is what decides whether it is night, and night is when kills pay more. So the minutes you spent dead cost you no night. Near the end of the night - the game's night ends at five in the morning - you could die repeatedly and keep the bonus that a living player would have lost. Measured: from half past four in the morning, forty deaths leave the very same creature paying 57 souls, where the identical stretch of time spent alive leaves it paying 42. Dying paid you 35 per cent more. That is exactly the kind of consolation prize this game is built never to give.

The reason nobody caught it is that the previous round compared the fixed game against the broken game, and never against a player who simply did not die. That comparison - same frames, alive - is the one that finds it.

The fix is a second clock. The world's clock still stops when you die, so your quest deadlines are still safe. But the clock that decides what a kill is worth keeps running whether you are alive or dead, and is reset to the world's clock every time you rest - so it can never drift far. The result is that dying now costs you nothing and pays you nothing: 42 against 42 at one end of the night, 57 against 57 at the other. Take the new clock back out and the unfairness comes straight back, in both directions. Meanwhile the deadline protection is untouched: forty deaths burn about a seventh of a second of world time with the fix in, and thirty-four minutes with the previous round's clock restored.

Two things I claimed in the last round turned out to be wrong, and both are now corrected in the code itself rather than only in a report. I had credited a change to how the bloodstain is drawn - lifting it onto the visible ground and giving it a glowing column - with making the bloodstain findable from every direction. It does not: with that change deleted the stain is still visible from all eight directions. The whole of that fix was a 19-centimetre correction to where the test camera's eye was, which had been sitting inside a boulder. What the drawing change does buy is a four- to sevenfold brighter reading, which is worth having and which a yes/no visibility count cannot see at all - so the check now scores that brightness against a floor, and deleting the drawing change turns the check red instead of leaving it green. The second wrong claim was that moving the camera's aim point mattered. It is worth nothing whatsoever.

Also reported rather than papered over: the design's fourth clause, 'any active timed quest has lost six hours', cannot be tested, because there are no timed quests in the game yet and the code that would fail one when its time runs out is never called by anything. Driven by hand it works perfectly. It simply has nothing wired to it.

And one honest no. One of the six conditions for the game being playable by its owner is reaching your first level-up without a test harness. It is not possible today, and this is measured rather than guessed: every one of the sixteen buttons the game defines was pressed, one at a time, from the world and from inside every screen it opens. They reach exactly two places - the world and your inventory. The game's own menu code advertises six destinations when you stand at a campfire, including the level-up screen, and five of the six have no door. That is one branch of code away from being fixed, but it belongs to the menu system rather than to this piece, so it is written down with the exact test it has to pass rather than changed here.

My own tool caught itself out twice on the way to that answer, which is worth recording: the first two versions of it pressed sixteen buttons and found nothing, both times because the presses were not landing rather than because the game had no door. Both wrong answers happened to be the right answer, which is the most dangerous way for a test to be broken.

headline: Every door in this game opened onto the same room, and walking through one did not change what was on your screen at all — the street stayed up while your body stood at the hearth, and walking back out left the room up while you stood in the road. All 115 doors did it. Both halves are fixed: the door now switches the picture on the frame you press it, and the picture is built from that building’s own file, so an alchemist’s shop in a dye town and a rotted great-hall in a village four kilometres away are no longer the same 249-triangle hall with different people standing in it.
detail:
This game has 115 named interiors — shops, inns, gaols, shrines, houses — behind 202 doors in eight towns. Two things were wrong with all of them at once, and the second one hid the first.

The first is the one that matters. Walking through a door did not change what was on your screen. The game correctly recorded that you were now inside The Crimson Apothecary, correctly moved your body to the spot just inside its door, and then carried on drawing the street. Walking back out was worse: your body was standing in the road and the screen was still showing the room. Every check the game had for this said it was fine, because every one of those checks asked where the player was, and the answer to that was always right. Nothing asked what was on the screen. All 115 doors did this; not one of them worked.

The second thing is that even if you forced the game to draw the room, there was only ever one room. 113 of the 115 interiors resolved to the same generic hall — the same hearth, the same six benches, the same beams — so an alchemist's shop in a dye town and a rotted Argonian great-hall in a village four kilometres away were the same picture with different people standing in it. Meanwhile the files describing those 115 rooms were extremely specific and completely unread: the apothecary's file lists 18 pieces of furniture, 10 lamps, a locked strongbox and one unique item, and the game drew a hearth and nothing else. Roughly two thousand pieces of furniture and thirty unique items existed only as text.

Both are fixed. Going through a door now switches the picture on the same frame you press the button, and going back out puts the street back. The room you arrive in is built from that building's own file: the walls are its real dimensions, the lamps are its real lamps in their real places, the furniture is its real furniture, and each of the eight towns has its own materials — Archon's dye-stained clay, Stormhold's legion blockwork, Helstrom's grown timber, Thorn's black needle-wood thatch — so two shops in two towns do not look alike. Rooms whose files mention a staircase get an upper floor. Shops big enough for one get a back room, because a shop that is one room with a counter is half a shop. The unique item each of 83 rooms declares is now a thing on a pedestal that you can walk up to and pick up.

The people were the other half. The game already moved them between rooms across the day — nine of Thorn's twenty-four change rooms between noon and three in the morning — but not one of them ever moved a millimetre. They were placed once when the town loaded and stayed there forever; a woman whose evening is spent at the tavern kept the position calculated inside her own house. The comment above that function claimed, in writing, that people "walk to the slot's anchor", and the function never touched anybody's position. Now it does: they cross the floor at walking pace when their day changes what they are doing, and they are put down where they belong when their day moves them to another building.

And they go outside. Before this, of the 347 people in the game, the only ones ever standing outdoors were 38 quest-givers belonging to another piece of work; at three in the morning there was not one person outdoors anywhere in the province, and none of this piece's own 260 townspeople ever stood on a street at any hour. Each of them now has a spot outside a real building's door in their own town, and a fifth of the day carved out to stand in it — a trading cohort out from nine to five, people going to and from work at the shoulders of the day, a group out in the evening, and a night watch, so that three in the morning is quiet rather than empty. 94 people are out at midday and 23 at 3 a.m., and the rest of everybody's day is untouched.

How I know it works rather than hope it does. The thing that let the first defect survive a whole round is that the tool checking it was made entirely out of the half that worked, so it could never have failed. That tool now reads the screen, and every new check in it is paired with a control that puts the old broken behaviour back and requires the reading to get worse: the sweep of all 115 doors is run twice, once normally and once with the connection cut, and the run passes only if the cut arm is worse. I also broke the tool that places people outdoors on purpose — shrinking a town to one metre across — and confirmed it refuses and names the fifteen people it can no longer place, then put the town back and checked that nothing was left changed in the repository.

Two things found on the way that were not what I was looking for. Rebuilding a room compiled new graphics shaders every time, which is a stutter at the exact moment a player presses a button on a doorstep, so rooms of the same type in the same town now share their materials. And the save file had never stored the outdoor station of a quest-giver at all, which meant every quest-giver came back from a saved game standing invisibly inside every locked cellar in the province — a bug from an earlier piece of work that only showed up because my own new field fell into the same hole.

Said plainly, what is not done: the outsides of the buildings. All 202 of them are still doors with nothing attached — the town's streets have no buildings drawn on them at all — so the townspeople this round put outdoors are standing on bare ground. That is the largest remaining piece and I did not attempt it.

headline: A blind taste test between our writing and Morrowind's turned out to be rigged by accident, and you could win it without reading a single word: just count the black bars. Every passage had its names blanked out to hide where it came from — and the real game's writing is so much denser with names that the blanks themselves gave the answer away, fifteen times out of fifteen.
detail:
The idea was simple and good. Take fifteen pairs of passages, one written for this project and one lifted from the real Morrowind, strip out every name so nobody can tell which is which, and hand them to a reader who has never seen either. If our writing is any good, a fair reader shouldn't be able to spot it.

The test had already been run once before and failed for an obvious reason: the real game's passages were full of words like Vvardenfell and Dunmer, so anyone could spot them instantly. So this round blanked out every name on both sides, replacing each with a marker like [NAME-7], and the person who built it re-ran the old cheat to prove it no longer worked.

It doesn't. But a new one does, and it is the same cheat wearing a hat. Morrowind's prose is thick with names — people, houses, towns, gods — and ours is mostly about offices, tides and ledgers. So after blanking, the real game's passages are covered in markers and ours are nearly clean. One pair had six markers on our side and thirty-nine on theirs. Another had forty-one against a hundred and twenty-nine. Count the markers, pick the sparser one, and you have identified our writing in all fifteen pairs without reading a sentence. Whatever that test was measuring, it wasn't quality.

Worse, the blanking tool is chewing the text while it works. It was mangling ordinary words it mistook for names — 'nevertheless', 'perhaps', 'sadly', even the letters of 'P.S.' — and dropping fragments as it went, so a line of Morrowind's arrived as 'said the landowner to the assembled ust not be doing so purely out of avarice'. Because that damage lands on whichever passage has more names in it, it always lands on the real game. The test was quietly vandalising the thing it was asking me to compare ours against.

And then the mistake I made myself, which is the part I'd rather record than bury. One pair put our writing against an old Morrowind story told as a letter. I marked the letter down for being a flat, plodding recap of events — a summary where there should have been a scene. Then the answers were revealed and I went back to it. The letter is dictated by a murderer standing over the body of the man whose name is signed at the bottom. The flatness is the murderer. Lines like 'It came as quite a surprise to her when he began strangling her' aren't lazy writing; they're a man being pleasant about a killing. I had marked down a voice for sounding exactly like the person it belonged to.

One more thing worth saying plainly, because it complicates the flattering version. I preferred our writing in fourteen of the fifteen pairs, which sounds like good news and mostly isn't — two thirds of what we were compared against wasn't really Morrowind's prose at all, but its quest log and its help text, the functional stuff written to keep a player from getting lost. Comparing a diary to a receipt and winning proves nothing. The honest finding runs the other way: a second reader and I, working separately, sorted the fifteen pairs into the same two piles every single time. Our writing is instantly recognisable, and the reason is that it has one habit and one voice. The habit is a see-saw sentence — 'He does not want the lease audited. He wants it laundered.' — and it turns up in nine of the fifteen. The voice is a dry, watchful, withholding official, and it is the voice of the magistrate, the trader, the swamp-dweller and the clerk alike. Morrowind's writing is worse than ours and more various than ours, and in a game where you meet forty people in an afternoon, the second thing may matter more than the first.

headline: Your money was never really your money. Selling stolen goods to a fence paid into one wallet, saving the game read from a second, and the inventory screen drew from a third that nothing ever filled — so it showed "0 gold" whether you had none or had just been handed 777. And training a lock-picking skill for hours never opened a single extra lock, because the number the locks actually check was frozen the day you started the game.
detail:
This piece covers the game's whole progression system — souls, levels, skills, carrying weight, gold — and it had never been worked on before today, so the first job was finding out what was actually true rather than assumed.

Gold turned out to be the worst of it. There were five different places in the code that each thought they were "how much gold the player has", and none of them talked to each other. Selling a stolen ring to a fence paid one of them. Paying a bribe spent a second. Buying a boat ticket spent a third, and because that third one gets rebuilt every time you rest or reload, a paid fare quietly refunded itself the next time you saved. The number the save file actually remembers is a fourth. And the screen that draws your inventory read a fifth field that nothing in the entire game ever writes to — which is why setting your gold to 777 and then looking at your own inventory still said zero. All five are now one number. Fencing, bribery, fares and the inventory screen all move the same purse, and a screenshot of the inventory after setting gold to 777 now genuinely shows 777.

Skills had a quieter version of the same problem. The game does track skill growth correctly — hit things with a sword and Blades goes up, pick a lock and Security goes up, and that part was already working. But the systems that are supposed to care about those numbers — which lock tiers you can pick, what a fence will pay you, how easily guards get suspicious of you — were all reading a second, private copy of your skills that got set once at the start of the game and never touched again, no matter how much you trained. A character who spent the whole game picking locks was, as far as every lock in the world was concerned, exactly as unskilled as the day they started. That copy now tracks the real one continuously, while still letting a scripted test pin a value on purpose when that's what the test needs.

Two things reported as already fixed by other work landed just before this piece started: the level-up screen used to offer ten attributes while the character underneath only had six, so three were unreachable and confirming certain choices invented brand-new, fictional attributes out of thin air. That is now genuinely resolved and was checked rather than taken on faith.

One big thing was found and deliberately left alone. A character's Strength, Intelligence and weapon skill are all supposed to affect how much damage a hit does — that's the whole point of a stat sheet. The formulas for it exist in the code, correctly written, and are called by nothing. Every weapon currently swings for the exact same damage regardless of the wielder's stats or skill. Fixing that properly means changing weapon data and the damage formula that another part of this project has spent many rounds carefully tuning, so instead of quietly breaking that work, it's written up and handed off with exact evidence of where the wiring is missing.

Also measured and left alone, correctly: carrying weight does slow you down when you're not fighting, and that's real and working. But the separate number that's supposed to make you roll worse in a fight when you're wearing heavy armour never reflects what you're actually wearing — it's stuck on a default. The mechanism that would react to it works fine; nothing feeds it a real number, and there's no armour-slot system yet for it to read from.

headline: Four problems other pieces found in the sneak-and-steal system this session, all confirmed and three fixed outright: loading a save left last session's onlookers standing in the new one, a bought-off guard cost real money that then vanished from your purse, some shops never locked their doors no matter the hour, and the streets people now walk at night were invisible to anyone trying to sneak past them.
detail:
This part of the game handles sneaking, theft, locks, witnesses and guards. Its own graded review two rounds ago found real problems and scored it a fail; this round was not about that review, it was about four specific claims other people working on the game made this session about defects in this system's area, each with a reason to believe rather than a guess. All four turned out to be real, and checking them properly meant reading the actual code rather than taking the claim at its word - one of the four turned out to already be half-fixed by someone else working at the same time, which was only discoverable by reading, not by assuming.

First: reloading a saved game did not clear out who was watching you. The list of nearby people, who they'd seen, and any in-progress search for a fugitive all belonged to whichever session was running before you clicked load, not to the save file you just opened. Fixed so a load now clears everyone in the room while leaving the actual crime record - your bounty, your stolen goods - exactly as the save says it should be.

Second: money. Selling stolen goods to a fence, bribing a witness, and paying off a bounty at a guard were all supposed to spend the same purse the save file writes down. The fence and the bribe already did, fixed by someone else earlier the same day. Paying off a guard did not: the deduction happened for exactly one instant and was silently undone the very next frame, so settling a bounty at the gate cost nothing at all against the money the game actually remembers you having. Now fixed the same way.

Third: a shop that is supposed to be locked at three in the morning sometimes wasn't, for no reason anyone had written down. Six shopkeepers in five different towns had their shop counted as part of their house rather than as its own building, so the game applied house hours - open all day, every day - to a room that was meant to keep a shop's. Measured directly: of the game's 66 rooms that are supposed to lock at night, 12 never did; now all 66 do.

Fourth, and the one worth a picture: a previous round of work this same session taught the townspeople to walk to work, come home, and stand outside at night instead of vanishing when nobody was looking at them. But the sneaking system - the part that decides whether someone sees you, hears you, or can be pickpocketed - had never been introduced to any of them. It had only ever been tested against people a scripted test put there by hand. In the actual, played game, a player creeping through a town at three in the morning had nobody real to sneak past. That is now wired together: anyone nearby and outdoors is a real target for the sneaking system, confirmed by asking the running game who it currently sees near the player in a town at that hour and getting back an actual person with a position, a direction they're facing, and whether they can presently see you - not an empty list.

One more thing was found but only partly fixed: the earlier graded review's single biggest complaint was that surrendering to a guard cost nothing, because the price was set to zero. That price is now a real number. What is still true, and said plainly rather than hidden, is that the guard still cannot fight back at all - that needs the game's enemy-behaviour system, which is somebody else's work and was itself being changed by another person at the same moment - so this is a partial answer to that complaint, not the whole one.

The game's shared files were being edited by dozens of people at once this session, hard enough that one change briefly vanished from disk and had to be re-checked and confirmed still present before this could be called done. Two of the four fixes above were confirmed inside the actual running game rather than only on paper before finishing.
