headline: The souls you take off a dead enemy now pay for exactly one thing - a level - and I checked every place in the code where they could have paid for anything else. There is no shop that takes them, no guard you can bribe with them, no toll. And a pile of gold, however big, will not buy you a level: I tried it with a hundred thousand coins and the game said no. The last round's embarrassment is gone too. Clearing the entire game used to leave you on level 120 exactly, which is the sort of round number that means somebody worked backwards from the answer. It now leaves you two-thirds of the way through level 93, which is what a number looks like when nobody was aiming at it.
detail:
This was a re-check of the reward system, and my job was to attack it rather than admire it, so here is what I found. The team fixed one bug twice - two separate safeguards, either of which is enough on its own. They tested them the sensible way, by removing one at a time, and both times the game carried on behaving perfectly, which they honestly reported as odd. It is odd, and it is worth understanding: I removed BOTH at once, and six live enemies immediately became worth nothing. So the fix is real. But each half looks useless when tested alone, and that is exactly how somebody deletes one next year believing it does nothing. That is now written down.

The bigger problem is arithmetic that has drifted apart. The reward system recently cut every enemy's value by about a third - a correction, and a good one. But the map's own file still lists the OLD values. It says the enemies scattered along the roads are worth 16,335 souls; they are worth 10,679. It says walking the whole road between the three towns and killing everything gets you to level 5; it gets you to level 3. Nothing anywhere checks these two files against each other, so the map has been quietly telling everyone a number that is half again too big. That is the one thing I have asked them to fix, and the fix is a single small checking tool.

I also looked hard at the headline evidence, which is a test advertised as trying 343 different sequences of events. It does run 343 - but they collapse into 14 genuinely different outcomes, nearly half of them pay nothing at all, and three of the seven kinds of event it shuffles are indistinguishable from each other. Every single one of those 343 passed; every problem it found came from two longer sequences outside that set. And all 463 of its runs use one enemy at one time of day, so the rule about enemies being worth more at night has never once been exercised by it. I checked that rule myself and it works - a fight worth 252 in the afternoon is worth 342 at eleven at night - but the test that claims to cover it does not.

Twice my own measuring tools were wrong in my favour and caught themselves, which I am reporting because it is the point of building them that way. One of them handed itself the souls it was supposed to earn by fighting, and passed a test designed to fail. The other read a character sheet in a practice arena that has no character in it, saw an empty page, and nearly accused the game of six faults it does not have. Score: 6 out of 10, below the bar of 7. No player would meet a broken thing here today. It is the difference between a system that is right and a system that has been shown to be right.

headline: The enemies in this game learned to fight this week - they circle, they fake a step in, they commit to a swing they cannot take back, and they walk home when you get away. I checked the part that matters most and it holds: I picked forty-seven swings and teleported the player forty metres away on the exact frame the sword started moving, and every single time the enemy finished the swing anyway. That is what a Souls enemy is. Then I checked whether it can actually catch you, and it cannot. If you simply WALK away - not run, walk - the guard follows at 2.2 metres a second against your 2.0, gains twenty centimetres a second, never breaks into a run because its rule for running is about distance rather than about whether it is gaining, gets no closer than eight metres in thirty seconds, hits the end of its leash and goes home. The road is still safe for anyone in no hurry. I also found that four of the seven enemies in the game are not just similar but the same fight: I recorded thirty seconds of a marsh sentry, a legion guard and two drowned men, and every position, every turn of the head and every choice of attack matched to the last decimal place - four names, four different amounts of health, one enemy. And the score the piece gave itself rests on a bookkeeping gap: the game never labels the moment after a swing as 'recovering', so the test that asks how much time an enemy spends standing on top of you throws those frames away. Count them and the number goes from 0.04 to 0.25. Eighty-five per cent of the time an enemy spends recovering from a swing, it is standing inside you.

You can ask anyone in this province about four hundred and sixty-eight subjects, and this week I found out that a hundred and fifty-one of them were written down where nobody could ever get at them. There was no way to bring them up. The words existed, somebody had written a rootkeeper's answer about egg-tending and a fisher's answer about the first tide, and no person in the game would ever say the noun that lets you ask. So I wrote the missing half of those conversations: sixty-odd answers, each one put in a particular person's mouth in a particular town, whose ordinary sentences happen to contain the subjects. Ask the Stormhold legionary about the cart roads and he names three of them, and now you can ask about those three. That is how Morrowind worked and it is why its world felt like it had corners you had not turned yet. I also found something worse and quieter: the towns' gossip could not change. Every settlement had eight rumours and they were the same eight in the last hour of the game as in the first, because the piece of code that picks a rumour looked at your race and where you were standing and never once at what had happened in the world. It was being handed the list of everything you had done and it was throwing it away. Now it reads it, and Lilmoth has twenty-four things to say when you arrive and thirty-two by the end, and some of the early ones stop being said. There are two hundred and thirty-nine rumours in the province now instead of eighty-three, and a dozen of them are wrong on purpose.

Every room in this game has lamps in it, and until today the part of the game that works out whether somebody can see you had never been told they were there. It was reading the WEATHER instead - so a windowless cellar at midday was as bright as an open field, and the same cellar at three in the morning was as dark as one, and it made no difference at all where in the room you stood. The lamps now light the room for the burglar as well as for the eye. Blow one out and the man watching you takes twice as long to notice you. And I measured what that is worth: steal the same thing from under the lamp and you get a 294 gold bounty, steal it from the dark corner of the same room and you get 118 - because in the dark they see somebody, but they cannot say who.
detail: Three things landed. FIRST, the lamps. The renderer has been drawing 827 authored interior lamps for weeks; the stealth model held zero of them, because the one function that adds a light had exactly one caller in the whole game and it was a test hook. It now reads the lamps out of the SAME file the renderer draws them from, so there is one list and it cannot drift. The brightness scale is worked out from the design document's own table rather than copied off the renderer. SECOND, the sleepers. The game's people have eight things they can be doing and not one of them is sleeping, so robbing a house at three in the morning was watched by every resident of it, wide awake, in the dark. Somebody at home between eleven at night and six in the morning is now asleep, and a sleeper is not a witness. I staged the same theft four ways to check - a witness in the room saw it and it cost 294 gold; one outside through a wall saw nothing; one asleep two metres away saw nothing; one watching from the dark corner saw somebody but could not name them, and it cost 118. THIRD, the theft. Every room has one unique object with an owner's name on it. You could pick all 83 of them up in front of their owners for free, because the button a player presses had never heard of ownership. It has now: 72 of the 83 are in the ownership system and taking one is a theft with a witness, a bounty and a fence who prices it as stolen goods. The other 11 have no owner written on them at all and I have said so rather than inventing one. I also cut both changes back out on a copy of the game and confirmed the old, wrong numbers come straight back - 0.75 everywhere, no theft, nothing stolen. And I counted the parameters in my own data files that nothing in the game reads: 116 out of 983, and I have listed every one.

headline: The province is meant to take about an hour to walk across. This week I sent a character to actually walk it, and he got thirty-nine metres. He was standing outside the capital with his nose against the wall of a house, and he stayed there for the next sixteen minutes of game time, because the main road out of Stormhold has been drawn straight through somebody's scribe. It turns out the roads and the towns are built by two different pieces of code that have never been introduced to each other: the road-builder lays out the highway over the bare landscape, and then the town-builder plants houses on the same ground, and nobody checks. I wrote the check. Every single one of the ten roads in the province goes through at least one building. Sixteen of those collisions are on the two big named journeys the game is measured by. To prove it really was the house and not something else, I picked the house up, moved it a kilometre east, and sent him again: he walked seven times further. Then I put the house back, and he stopped in exactly the same spot, to the tenth of a metre. I also found that the instrument the project uses to check the walk is honest only looks at one frame in every six, and something is moving the character on the other five - when he is standing perfectly still the two numbers agree exactly, and when he is moving they disagree by a factor of three and a half. And a separate one: nineteen dangers are scattered around the province, and six of them are traps. The game had been telling itself that a trap which had just gone off had not gone off, because it was asking whether the trap was still armed instead of whether anything had happened to you. One of those six kills you outright, and the report said nothing had happened.

Armour is heavy, and until today you could not put any on. The game has always shipped a chitin cuirass, legion greaves, a hauberk, boots and a cowl, each with a weight written on it, and each one you tried to wear went into your sword hand instead - because the only place the code knew how to put a thing you equipped was the right fist. That mattered more than it sounds. The whole point of armour in a game like this is the trade: heavier gear means a slower, shorter dodge with a smaller window where the blow passes through you, and that window is the thing your hands learn first. It was implemented, exactly and correctly, and nothing you could do in the world reached it - the number it read off was a constant somebody typed in. So you now dress the character and the dodge changes. Wearing nothing, the roll is invulnerable for 26 frames out of 52. Put on the heaviest set the game currently owns - about 28 kilos - and it drops to 22 out of 60, and the recovery afterwards, the part where you are lying on the floor and can be hit, goes from 22 frames to 34. Carrying is a separate question from wearing, and deliberately so: four hundred and sixty kilos of looted hammers in your pack does not change your dodge by a single frame. What it changes is the walk home. Loaded up you move at 72% speed, you cannot run, and the barge that took forty minutes of game time now takes fifty-four - same boat, same fare, longer day. You cannot carry a dungeon out in one trip, which is the whole reason the merchants have limited money. I also counted, for every number these two systems publish, whether anything in the running game actually reads it. Twenty-six numbers; twenty-two are read; four are not - what the weight does to your stamina outside a fight, to how easily guards spot you, to how high you jump, and to how much a fall hurts. Those four are written down and named rather than quietly left. And one small ugly thing found by accident: a tool the project uses to test carrying weight had stopped working months ago - it set the weight and the game overwrote it a sixtieth of a second later - so anything measured with it since then needs taking again.

The quests in this game keep asking the player to know something before they will let you settle them peacefully - that the shortfall in the wells started before the tree-cutters arrived, that the seal on a paper is in the wrong wax, that four of the eleven doors in the shut quarter have been chalked. For 121 of those demands the quest files name exactly where you find out. Sixty-three of them named a thing that did not exist. There was no ledger to read, no letter, no mark on any wall - the game asked you to have learned something from a book nobody had written. So I wrote them. Twenty-six documents, about nine thousand seven hundred words: a prison book of torn lease counterfoils where the word again is written four times against the same twelve people, a wharf fund kept in pencil on a scrap because ink runs in a wet shed, a letter from a daughter at Soulrest asking why her dead father voted in the spring. And twenty-five things to look at, standing in the world where the fact is: eleven chalk marks on eleven jambs, four water marks over a reach bed, a post in the Helstrom gallery with nobody on it. Reaching for one of them opens no window and prints no sentence at you - you looked at the thing, and your journal knows it now. Demanded truths a player can actually reach: 58 of 121, now 100. Played through the browser, the main quest used to stop dead at its sixth job because the ledger it wanted was not in the building; it now runs twenty-eight jobs deep and stops on a choice you made earlier, which is the kind of stopping a story is supposed to do.

The game kept two separate notes of how much the world is worth in souls, and they disagreed by half again — 16,335 against 10,679. One of them was the price list the game actually pays out from; the other was a summary written down once and never updated. Nothing had ever compared them. The road you walk from the first town to the last was advertised as buying you level 5. It buys you level 3.
detail: Souls are what you get for killing something and the only thing you can spend them on is a level. Each enemy carries its own price tag, and a separate file kept a running total of everything standing in the province — how much each roadside camp is worth, how much each region is worth, and what clearing the main road would pay you. Last night the prices were re-worked, seven of them, and the running total was never recalculated. So for a day the world published one number and paid another, and every summary line in that file was 53% too generous. Which of the two is right is not a matter of taste: we followed a real kill through the code and then through the running game, deliberately telling the summary file a lie (this camp is worth 73 souls) and killing the enemies in it. The player was paid 22 — the price on the enemies themselves, to the soul. So the summary was regenerated from the price tags, and there is now a check that reads BOTH files and fails the build the moment they disagree. It runs on every commit that touches game data, so nobody has to remember it. We proved it can fail three ways: on the old stale file it goes red and names the exact rows; move one enemy price by a single soul and it goes red again; delete the check itself and the build says so rather than going quiet. The one number that changed for a player: clearing the whole Stormhold-to-Lilmoth road was advertised at level 5 and pays level 3. We have not touched what anything is worth — that is a different job, and a reviewer graded it an hour ago. Evidence: reports/w1-souls-ledger/reconciliation.json and reports/w1-souls-ledger/consumption.json; the gap was named by corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-SOULS-r3.md section 9.

headline: Two books in this game disagree about a drowning. An Imperial prefect, who was four years old when it happened, has read a four-word note in an army day-book — 'halted near bank. line formed' — and decided there must have been a battle. A weir-woman upriver answers him: there was no battle, there were twenty of us sitting down on a rock in plain sight with nothing in our hands, and a line is what you form when you do not know. Neither of them is corrected. Nobody in the game ever tells you who was right. That is exactly how it is supposed to work — and then I checked whether a player can find either book, and the answer is no. Neither one is shelved anywhere in the world. Of the nineteen arguments the library is built around, a player can reach both sides of three. The best writing in this project is sitting in a folder that the game can read and the player cannot walk to.

Somebody wrote a House Dres magister for this game and he is very good. Asked about a column of soldiers who drowned at a ford, he says: “If a column had been lost at that ford, provincial, House Dres would have a record of it. House Dres has a record of it.” There are twenty-three lines like that, and not one of them can ever be spoken, because there is no magister anywhere in the province to say them. The lines are addressed to a job title nobody in the world holds. I measured the whole of it: a tenth of the dialogue in this build — 133 answers out of 1,280 — cannot be reached by any character you could make, standing in front of any person there is. The tool that was supposed to catch that reported three.
detail: This was a review of the talking. The good news first, because it is most of the news: the writing is the best in the project and I could not break it. I read a couple of hundred lines looking for the usual failures — characters who exist to point you at your next task, everybody sounding like the same author, dialogue that helpfully tells you where to go — and did not find them. A healer describing a marsh people walk into and do not walk out of says ‘The ones who don’t come out are not the ones I think about’, and then tells you nothing about where it is or why you would go. A clerk asked about a wall gives you two pieces of paperwork that cancel each other out. Across fifty thousand words there are six lines in the whole game that end by telling you where to go, which is about the same rate as Morrowind itself. I also built a tool specifically to catch one writer doing six accents, ran it, and it said I was wrong — the quiet characters stay quiet even in the newest file. That is a real result and it belongs at the top. The bad news is the join between the writing and the game. Every line is stamped with who is allowed to say it — a job (‘magister’, ‘notary’, ‘harbourmistress’) and sometimes a town. Nobody had ever checked those stamps against the list of people who actually exist. Forty lines are addressed to jobs no one holds; ninety more are addressed to a job in a town where nobody of that job stands. The near-misses are the ones that sting: there IS a notary in the game, and she is filed under ‘archivist’, so her six lines never reach her. There is a topic called ‘magister varo dren’ whose answer is ‘I am he’, and Varo Dren is not in the game at all. Why did nobody notice? Because the checker and the game disagree about a rule. Morrowind picks the first answer that fits; this build picks the most specific one. The checker was written for Morrowind’s rule. I measured that the difference never comes up — in seventy-six thousand conversations, not once does the order of the answers decide anything — which also means a tidy-up job this round that reordered them, and was proudly reported as having changed nothing, could not possibly have changed anything. It was true and it was not evidence. I wrote four tools for this review and deliberately broke each one first to make sure it could go red. One more thing worth saying out loud, because it is the same shape as the headline: thirteen answers in the game carry an instruction to open a journal entry when you ask about them, and the code that reads answers throws that instruction away without looking at it. Score 5 out of 10 against a bar of 7, which is a fail, and a reader who takes that as ‘mediocre’ will have the wrong idea in both directions. Full reasoning, with the lines quoted: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-17-r1.md

headline: You can now summon a bigger monster, and frighten one further away. Both of those sound like things a game already does, and neither was true here. The spell-making screen let you dial a summon up to ninety points of strength and charged you for every one of them, but the thing that hauled itself out of the water was the same 260-hit-point creature every time. A fright spell said in its own notes that it "drives a target to flee", and then left the target standing exactly where it was — motionless, and indistinguishable from the calming spell next to it. So we built a tool that turns every dial on all fifty-five spell effects, one at a time, and asks whether the world notices. Of the 104 dials the game offers you, 26 were connected to nothing at all. Three of them are now wired up. A weak summon dies in two seconds and does 41 damage to you; a strong one shrugs off a beating and does 164. A lightly frightened creature stops running after six metres; a badly frightened one runs forty-five. To prove we had not fooled ourselves, we cut our own changes back out on a scratch copy and re-ran everything: the weak and strong summons went back to being identical, and the frightened creature went back to standing still at exactly the distance the calmed one does. The other 23 dead dials are written down by name, so the next person does not have to find them again.

The game finally lets your armour decide how well you dodge — and it still cannot see the sword and shield in your hands. I put a character in the heaviest weapon and the heaviest shield the game has, and the encumbrance meter read zero. Not "a bit light". Zero. Then I swapped the sword for the biggest one in the game, twenty kilos of it, and the number that decides your dodge did not move by a single digit out of six decimal places.
detail: In this game, how much you are wearing decides how good your dodge roll is — how many frames you spend invulnerable, how long you are stuck at the end of it. That is the Dark Souls half of the design and it is meant to be the most legible decision you make. Until this round, nothing you wore reached it at all: the number was frozen at 24% no matter what, so every dodge measurement anyone had ever taken was taken against a character wearing an imaginary outfit. This round built the missing connection and it genuinely works. I checked it by switching the fix back off in the running game and watching the old broken number come back exactly, twice, in both orders. I also checked the thing that would have been worst to get wrong: your rucksack must NOT affect your dodge, because a fight should not depend on how much loot you happen to be hauling. I put 460 kilograms of iron mauls in the bag and the dodge came back frame-for-frame identical. That is exactly right and it is the hardest part to keep right. But the connection only looks at clothes. It reads the shirt, trousers, boots, hat and belt — and not the weapon or the shield, which are the first two things anyone would think of. The weights are already sitting in the game's own files, fifteen weapons from a one-kilo dagger to a twenty-kilo greatsword, and no part of the game has ever read them. Worse, the game turns out to have two right hands: put a warhammer on and it gets counted for weight while your character carries on swinging the sword they had before. And because clothes are all that counts, the heaviest outfit the game can currently dress you in comes to sixteen kilos — which is not enough to leave the lightest of the four dodge categories. Three of the four exist only if a tester types the number in by hand. Score 3 out of 10 against a bar of 7. The fix does not need anyone to invent a single new number: the weights are already there, they just need reading.

headline: When you want to know whether something in the game actually works, the honest way to check is to break it on purpose and see if your test notices. Run it once with the thing working, once with it broken, and if both runs give you the same answer then your test was never watching. Three separate people on this project did exactly that check this week, all three tests came back green, and all three were measuring nothing. In one, the switch that was supposed to take the walls out of a town did not take them out, so fifteen walks into a wall were compared against fifteen identical walks into the same wall. In another, one repair had been made twice over, so removing either half on its own changed nothing and both halves looked like dead code — the next person along would have deleted one in good faith and put the bug back. In the third, the test compared how many townspeople moved overnight against a control town that had nobody living in it at all: nought against nought, and it passed. So we built one shared piece of machinery that does this properly for the whole project. You hand it a measurement and a list of ways to break it; it tries every combination, counts how many things it was actually looking at, and fails whenever the two runs agree. Then we pointed it at the three real cases and it caught all three, going red on the broken versions and green on the fixed ones, using nothing but the files those people had already left behind. It also has to prove it can fail: we sabotage the checker itself three ways, and it has to notice each one. It does. Along the way we ran two things the project had written down and never once executed. One is a register of fifteen things a player is deliberately allowed to get away with — brewing a potion that makes the next potion stronger, wearing the wrong uniform past a patrol, selling the quest item — each with a test that goes red the day someone quietly closes it. Thirteen still stand, two cannot be tested because the thing they need was never built, and we proved the alarm works by sneaking a closure in and watching it fire. The other is a grid of which of the game's nineteen systems are supposed to touch each other, forty-one of those crossings being the ones that matter — the sort of thing where a book you read in hour two tells you a boss's weakness in hour nine. Only four of the forty-one have any data behind them at all. And the one long recording of somebody actually playing this game — ten minutes, eighty-two megabytes — contains not a single event. Nothing happened, or nothing was written down; either way there is currently nothing for a player to tell a friend about afterwards, and that is the number this whole area exists to move.

The lamps in this game are finally connected to the thing that decides whether a guard can see you — that was the round's big claim and I could not break it. Standing next to a hearth and standing in the black corner behind it are now genuinely different, and blowing out one oil lamp doubles the time it takes an enemy to notice you. But there are eleven rooms in the province where the fix points the wrong way. Nobody ever wrote any lamps into those rooms, so the part that draws them quietly invents a fire so you aren't staring at a black screen — and the part that decides whether you're hidden doesn't, and rates the room as pitch dark. I took a picture of one: a lit fireplace, two windows bright enough to read by, three people you can see clearly, and the game thinks you're invisible.
detail: I checked five claims and re-ran every headline number myself rather than taking the builder's word. The big one holds up exactly: eight lamps in a shop where there used to be none, and the same brightness pattern at midday and at three in the morning, which is what it should look like when a room is lit by fire instead of by the sky. Blowing out a lamp takes an enemy from noticing you in forty frames to eighty. All of that is real and it is the largest single improvement this system has had. Three things went the other way. First, the drawing code and the hiding code disagree about which lamps are actually burning — the drawing code lights at most five per room to keep the frame rate up, the hiding code lights all fourteen if there are fourteen. Across every interior in the game that is about seven percent of the indoor floor where what you can see and what the game thinks you can see are different, and most of it is those eleven rooms. Second, and this is the one I would fix first: you can steal a chair out of somebody's house and sell it to the fence in that same town, and he pays you exactly what he'd pay for an honest chair. Somebody wrote him a line for that moment — 'That belongs to Ahnassi Dark-Water of terraces. I drink with Ahnassi Dark-Water of terraces. Take it elsewhere.' — and he can never say it, because the code that asks him hands him a blank list of townspeople instead of the real one. It affects 1,787 of the 1,950 owned objects in the world. Third, the round fixed a bug where the lamps were only ever put in by test code and never by the game, and left the identical bug next door: the hiding places an NPC checks when it loses you are also only ever put in by test code, so a guard who loses your trail walks to where he last saw you, stands there for two seconds and gives up. I also ran an experiment the round didn't: its fix had two separate edits, and nobody had tested them apart. Doing so shows the lamps alone don't actually make the room interesting — what does the work is the separate decision that indoors is dark, and that decision was justified by a windowless cellar. There are no cellars in this game. There are 112 rooms with windows. Score 0 out of 10 on the harshest scale, 2.7 on the same scale the last review used, which scored 3.0 — the number went down because I proved the fence's refusals don't work and the last review had given them credit. Full reasoning: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-15-r3.md

headline: Half the truths this game asks you to discover had nothing to discover them from — no ledger, no letter, no mark on a wall — and this round wrote them. Twenty-six documents, nearly ten thousand words of prison counterfoils, toll chits and a letter from a dead man's daughter, plus twenty-five things standing in the world you can walk up to and look at. I checked the central claim with my own tools rather than theirs and it holds: a hundred of a hundred and twenty-one now have a route, the main quest gets from five quests deep to twenty-eight, and when I deliberately broke the code that lets you look at a mark, the same four tests went from all passing to all failing. The writing is genuinely good. But it has habits: nineteen of the twenty-six documents end by telling you where the paper is kept and whether the drawer is locked, all eight of the questions in the whole collection are the same short pointed question in eight different mouths, and one ledger does the reader's arithmetic for them in a voice that belongs to nobody in the document. And the list the round left behind of the eleven people still missing from the game names three who aren't blocking anything and leaves out three who are.
detail: Six things were checked. (1) The prose, read end to end. The Blackrose lease stubs — where a clerk has written the word 'again' four times against the same twelve people and a later clerk rules the total at four hundred and eleven and initials it so the next one knows it is a real count — are excellent, and the arithmetic checks to the digit. Against the project's own measured yardstick, though, the word 'four' appears in seventy-seven percent of the twenty-six documents and 'eleven' in thirty-one percent, where the real Morrowind books measured for comparison use 'eleven' in under three percent. The prose checker passes the file because its rule for that was deliberately narrowed years of rounds ago and never covered 'four'. (2) The claim most likely to be wrong: a leftover line in an old measuring tool that hands the game answers it should have to earn. It turns out that tool was never used for the headline number, and I proved with a fresh tool that switching the line off changes nothing anyway. (3) The headline number itself came from the builder's own instrument, so I built a different one that plays the whole main quest through the real game logic with no browser at all — two of the three published figures came back identical, to the same quest and the same missing fact. The third didn't, and the gap turned out to be my tool's, not theirs, which I say so. (4) The proof that the world actually reads any of this: re-run, four of four, and zero of three once I broke it on a copy. (5) The twenty-one truths still unreachable: count confirmed exactly, composition corrected. Seven of the nine that need eavesdropping already have the people; only two need writing. (6) Two bugs the round found in a browser and fixed — one where documents got stacked so close together that pressing the button opened the wrong one, another where every reset left the world with no marks in it at all. Both hold: I checked all eighty-three rooms in the game and six resets in a row rather than one. Along the way I found that the little pixel font nine of this project's chart tools share is broken in a way nobody had noticed: two dots are missing from the middle of every letter and number, which slides everything below them sideways. The round reported it for its own chart and fixed its digits, but it is in nine tools, and in the round's own published picture the word BOOK reads as POOK. Score 6.5 against a bar of 7 — a near miss on a strong round, failing on a hand-off list built from the wrong query and a reporting bug that was found, half-diagnosed and never scoped. Full reasoning: corpus/90-verdicts/wave1/W1-READABLES-r2.md

headline: The rulebook and the game disagreed about how an NPC picks what to say, and nobody had noticed that every tool built to check the dialogue was checking the rulebook's version. Morrowind's rule is simple: the writers put the answers in an order and the game reads down the list and takes the first one that fits the person you are. Ours quietly scored each answer for how specific it was and took the highest. Most of the time those agree — the writers had already put the fussiest answers first — but on eight subjects, from the price of a room in Stormhold to who really witnessed a killing in Gideon, the game overrules the writer and says something else. I measured it properly for the first time: 1.9 million of 1.46 billion possible conversations come out differently, which is 37 places in the world where a specific person gives a specific wrong answer. The ruling is that the game changes, not the rulebook, because dialogue is Morrowind's to own. The bigger discovery is what this made invisible. A tool had been run to tidy the order of every answer file, and it reported that it changed nothing, and that was treated as proof it was safe. It could not have changed anything: under the scoring rule the order only matters in one topic in the whole province. The reassuring zero was guaranteed before the tool ran. Once the game follows the writers' order, shuffling it moves 18% of all conversations — so the same check finally means something. There is a test now that a future writer can run to see whether the game and the rulebook still agree, and I broke it on purpose to prove it goes red. Separately, and worse: thirteen conversations were written to open a journal entry when you ask about them, and nothing in the game reads that instruction. Delete it entirely and not one word changes anywhere. That is the twentieth thing this project has found that was carefully written and plugged into nothing.

I sat down and actually played the opening the way you would — I opened the page with no special settings, pressed the keys, and nothing else. The good news is real: the title screen comes up, you press New, and you are standing in the hold of a prison barge in third person with a woman on the other bench, a knife on the floor, and not one word of explanation anywhere. You can walk around for as long as you like and nobody asks you anything; she only speaks when you go over and reach for her, which is exactly the trick Morrowind's famous opening pulls. Then it falls over twice. When you type your name, fourteen of the twenty-six letters are silently swallowed, because those keys are also the buttons for walking and swinging a sword — so I typed "Silt-Under-Salt" and the game wrote down "il-Un" — and the letter E is the talk button, so typing it ends the conversation in the middle of your own name. And when you walk up to the clerk who is supposed to write you into the province's records, the game stops dead: nothing ever told it what species you are, so the clerk repeats an internal error message at you forever and the door out is locked until she has written you down. Every impressive number this part of the game has ever reported was measured through a back door that fills in that missing detail automatically, so nobody had noticed. Both are small repairs, and the writing they are hiding is genuinely better than the game it is chasing.
detail: W1-26 round 2 verdict: FAIL 1.3/10 (RI-JRN09 2, RI-JRN01 2, RI-EXP01 0), unchanged from round 1 for entirely different reasons. Round 1's biggest gap is closed and O6 — control before definition — is repaired and measures 61.5 s against a 60 s bar. Three new caps: creation cannot be completed from the title (censusBegin({}) never observes a race); text entry is shadowed by the control map; and DTR 0.000 at hold.out, where Jeeh-Ei's reply to your name is drawn in the next room by the wrong speaker.

headline: A tenth of the best writing in this game could not be heard by anybody. Not badly written, not hidden behind a hard quest - simply addressed to people who did not exist. One hundred and thirty-six lines of dialogue were written for a Gideon records-clerk, a Stormhold sap-buyer, a Lilmoth gravedigger and a House Dres magister, and when we went to look, the province had no such people in it. The magister was the worst of it: twenty-three lines, some of the sharpest in the whole script, written for a man the story names out loud - you can ask about Varo Dren and the answer is 'I am he' - and Varo Dren had never been put into the world. Nobody could say it back to you. So this round did not write a single new line. It gave the existing ones mouths. Twenty-two people were added to the towns their lines were already written for, and twenty more lines were handed to somebody who was standing there all along under a different job title - the notary who was filed as an archivist, the harbourmistress filed as a clerk. One hundred and thirty of the hundred and thirty-six can now be heard by a real player standing in front of a real person. We also had to fix the measuring tape twice on the way: the tool that counts unheard lines was quietly confusing unrelated topics with each other, and the tool that checks each character type has its own verbal tic was only reading half of what it was told to read - which had made one archetype look broken when it was fine. And we deleted thirteen lines of machinery that was supposed to open a quest journal when you asked about something, because it pointed at thirteen quests nobody ever wrote.

The main road out of the capital ran straight through a scribe's house, and it had done since the day both were built. Two different pieces of the world-builder were responsible: one drew the roads across the landscape, the other put the towns down afterwards, and neither of them had ever been shown the other's work. Nobody had noticed because each was doing its own job perfectly well - the road was a good road, the house was a good house, and the wall between them only existed for anyone actually trying to walk past. Which is what we finally did: we put a body on the province's headline journey, the hour-long walk from Stormhold to Lilmoth, and it got thirty-nine metres before it stopped dead against somebody's back wall and stood there for sixteen simulated minutes. All ten roads in the province had the same problem somewhere along them. The fix was to decide which side gives way, and we chose the road: a town is where it is for reasons, a road is only ever a way of getting somewhere. So the road-builder now reads the town plans before it lays anything down, and wherever a road comes within fifty-five metres of a building it re-cuts that stretch on a one-metre grid with the houses treated as walls. Crucially it does not swing wide around the town, which would have been a worse world than the bug - it threads between the houses and becomes the street, the way a road does in Morrowind. The whole detour costs ninety-five metres on a seven-kilometre crossing, about forty-eight seconds of walking. Ten roads out of ten are now clear, and the body walks five hundred and fifty metres instead of thirty-nine. It still does not reach Lilmoth: past the capital it climbs the Valus Ridge and slips off the edge of the road onto a fifty-seven-degree hillside it cannot climb back up. That is a separate and older fault - the same steep stretches were on the old road too - and nobody had ever got past the wall to find it.

The province had a hundred and fifty-two books in it and ninety-nine of them were in no room, no shelf, no pocket and no hand. They existed only as files. The best writing in this project is a pair of accounts of the same afternoon at a river crossing - an Imperial prefect who was four years old when it happened, building a battle out of four words in somebody's day-book, and a weir-woman answering him with 'a line is what you form when you do not know' - and a player could not have read either one. Nineteen arguments are formally registered in this game as arguments, two books each, deliberately disagreeing. You could get to both sides of three of them. Now you can get to both sides of all nineteen, because ninety-nine texts have been put into forty rooms that already existed, on the rule that a book lives where its argument is had rather than in a library: the army's standing instruction is in the Stormhold garrison and the sergeant who thinks it is nonsense wrote his answer in the back of his own book in a different town's guardhouse. The Empire's pamphlet about how happy everyone is sits in the customs house that hands it out, and the salt-factor's private ledger, which is the answer to it, sits in another building across the town. We proved it the only way that counts: walk in, stand at the shelf, press the button a player presses, and watch the right book open - then take the placements out again on a copy and watch the shelf be empty. The second thing was the names. More than half the Argonians in this game were called things like Falura Nine-Teeth, which is a Dark Elf first name bolted to an English nickname, and one of them was 'Sedura Nine-Teeth' - sedura is a Dark Elf honorific, so the town roster contained an Argonian called Sir Nine-Teeth. Forty-three names were being worn by more than one person, one of them by six people in five different towns, and eighteen had a bit of the generator's plumbing still showing in them ('of salvage yard', with no 'the'). Argonians in the source material have names in their own language, and the descriptive nicknames are a minority form - eleven percent of the real ones. Ours were fifty-six percent. They are now ten, every coined name built out of the project's own root-list and passed through the project's own phonology checker, and every name that was written by a human being was left exactly alone. And we wrote eleven small things the library did not have: six songs and five children's stories, including a toll clerk's tariff set to forced rhyme, a lullaby out of the plague years that two households end differently, and the story of the girl on the Soulrest steps who carried a full jar up all forty of them for thirty years without spilling and is in none of the Chapter's books.
